Modern farming faces the challenge of feeding a growing population while protecting soil, water and biodiversity. In Azerbaijan, farmers grow cotton, wheat, tea in the Lankaran region, fruits such as pomegranates and persimmons, and hazelnuts, which are an important export.

articles.title: The Water Cycle
articles.description: The endless journey of water around the planet.
articles.content:
The water cycle is the continuous movement of water on, above and below the surface of the Earth. It is powered by the Sun's energy and by gravity.

Water evaporates from oceans, lakes and rivers and is released by plants through transpiration. As the vapour rises and cools, it condenses into clouds, and eventually falls as rain, snow or hail, called precipitation. The water then flows over the land as rivers, soaks into the ground as groundwater, or freezes in glaciers, before returning to the sea.

About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water, and of the 3% that is fresh, most is locked in ice, leaving only a tiny fraction easily available in rivers, lakes and groundwater. The same water has been recycled for billions of years.

articles.title: The Absheron Peninsula
articles.description: The windswept Caspian peninsula of Baku and the eternal fires.
articles.content:
The Absheron Peninsula is a narrow peninsula about 60 kilometres long that projects from the Caucasus into the Caspian Sea. Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan, and the city of Sumgait are located on it, and about a third of the country's population lives there.

The landscape is dry and windswept, with a semi-desert climate, salt lakes and low hills. Oil has seeped from the ground here for thousands of years, and mud volcanoes and natural gas vents are common. This is the origin of the fires that gave the name Land of Fire: the Ateshgah temple in Surakhani was a place of worship for fire-worshippers, and at Yanar Dag a hillside has burned continuously for decades.

Absheron has ancient fortresses, such as those in Mardakan, and sandy beaches along the sea. Its oil derricks and wind farms symbolise the region's past and future energy.

articles.title: Mount Bazarduzu
articles.description: The highest peak of Azerbaijan.
articles.content:
Mount Bazarduzu, also spelt Bazardüzü, is the highest peak in Azerbaijan, at 4,466 metres. It lies in the Greater Caucasus on the border with Russia's republic of Dagestan and is the country's most famous mountain.

The name means market square. Its steep slopes are covered by snow and small glaciers for much of the year, and climbers reach the summit in summer. It is near the ski resorts of Shahdag and Tufandag, which have made the mountain region a popular destination.

The surrounding areas hold Alpine meadows, and villages such as Khinalig and Laza, home to distinct communities with their own languages. Wild goats and brown bears live in the Caucasus.

articles.title: Lake Goygol
articles.description: The blue mountain lake formed by an earthquake.
articles.content:
Lake Goygol, which means blue lake, is a mountain lake in western Azerbaijan, near the city of Goygol, in the Lesser Caucasus. It is surrounded by pine and beech forests and is one of the most beautiful spots in the country.

The lake was formed in 1139 when a powerful earthquake caused a huge landslide from Mount Kapaz that blocked the Ağsu river valley. The water rose behind the natural dam, drowning the valley and creating several lakes. Goygol is the largest of them and was named a national park in 2008.

In the 19th century German settlers founded the village of Helenendorf, now Goygol, nearby and made wine there. Today visitors come for the lake, hiking trails and the fresh mountain air.

articles.title: The Mingachevir Reservoir
articles.description: The Sea of Mingachevir, the biggest lake in the Caucasus.
articles.content:
The Mingachevir Reservoir is the largest artificial lake in Azerbaijan and the South Caucasus, and it is often called the Sea of Mingachevir. It was created on the Kura River in 1953 by a large dam built beside the city of Mingachevir.

The reservoir covers about 600 square kilometres and holds around 16 cubic kilometres of water. It feeds the Mingachevir hydroelectric power station, the largest in the region, and water from it irrigates thousands of hectares of farmland in the dry Kura-Aras Lowland.

The lake is also used for fishing and recreation, with beaches on its shores. It has played a large role in the development of the region, but dams such as this one changed the natural flow of the Kura and affect migrating fish such as sturgeon.

articles.title: Nakhchivan
articles.description: Azerbaijan's mountainous exclave.
articles.content:
Nakhchivan is an autonomous republic of Azerbaijan, separated from the rest of the country by a strip of Armenian territory. It has an area of about 5,500 square kilometres and a population of around 460,000, and borders Armenia, Iran and Turkey. Its capital is the city of Nakhchivan.

The land is mountainous and dry, with the Zangezur and Daralayaz ranges and a peak of about 3,900 metres, Mount Kapıjik. The Aras River flows along the border. The region is one of the oldest inhabited places in the Caucasus, and legend says that the Prophet Noah's tomb is in the city.

Historic sites include the Momine Khatun Mausoleum, built in 1186, and Alinja Castle. The Duzdag salt mine, with its underground salt caves, is used to treat asthma and other breathing problems.

articles.title: The Lankaran Lowland
articles.description: Azerbaijan's humid subtropical south.
articles.content:
The Lankaran Lowland is a narrow coastal plain in south-eastern Azerbaijan, between the Caspian Sea and the Talysh Mountains, along the border with Iran. It has a humid subtropical climate, the wettest in the country, and receives more than 1,000 millimetres of rain a year.

The mild, wet weather allows the growing of tea, citrus fruit, rice, vegetables and early spring crops that are not grown elsewhere in the country. Tea has been cultivated there since the early 20th century. The region's capital is the city of Lankaran, and the Talysh people, who have their own language, live here.

The slopes of the Talysh Mountains are covered by Hyrcanian forests, a survivor from ancient times, in Hirkan National Park. Its warm mineral springs and beaches attract visitors.

articles.title: The Kura–Aras Lowland
articles.description: The largest plain in Azerbaijan.
articles.content:
The Kura–Aras Lowland is the largest plain in Azerbaijan, in the centre and south-east of the country, between the Greater and Lesser Caucasus and the Caspian Sea. It is formed by the sediment deposited by the Kura and Aras rivers, and includes the Mil, Mugan and Shirvan plains.

Parts of the lowland lie below sea level, since the Caspian itself is 28 metres below the ocean. The climate is dry, with hot summers and mild winters, so irrigation is essential. Cotton, grain, vegetables and fruit are grown there, and the winter pastures were used for centuries by herders who moved their flocks down from the mountains.

The Shirvan National Park, in the lowland, protects the goitered gazelle, or jeyran, and thousands of migratory birds winter in its wetlands. The region holds the main cities of Sabirabad, Salyan and Imishli.

articles.title: The Bosphorus
articles.description: The strait that divides Istanbul and Europe from Asia.
articles.content:
The Bosphorus is a narrow strait in Turkey, about 31 kilometres long, that connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and separates the European and Asian parts of Istanbul. At its narrowest it is only about 700 metres wide.

It is one of the world's busiest and trickiest waterways, and along with the Dardanelles is the only route from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. The Montreux Convention of 1936 governs passage through the straits. Three suspension bridges span the Bosphorus, and a railway tunnel, Marmaray, runs beneath it.

The strait's shores are lined with palaces, such as Dolmabahçe, old wooden mansions called yalıs, fortresses and mosques. Ferries carry commuters between continents. The city of Byzantium, later Constantinople, grew here because of its control of the passage.

articles.title: The Suez Canal
articles.description: The shortcut between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
articles.content:
The Suez Canal is an artificial waterway in Egypt, about 193 kilometres long, that connects the Mediterranean Sea at Port Said with the Red Sea at Suez. It was built by the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps and opened in 1869.

It allows ships to travel between Europe and Asia without sailing around Africa, saving about 7,000 kilometres on the trip between London and Mumbai. It has no locks, since the Mediterranean and Red Sea are at nearly the same level. About 12% of world trade passes through it, and Egypt earns large sums in tolls.

In 2015 a new parallel channel was opened to allow two-way traffic on part of the route. In 2021 the container ship Ever Given ran aground and blocked the canal for six days, showing how important it is to global shipping.

articles.title: The Strait of Gibraltar
articles.description: The gateway between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
articles.content:
The Strait of Gibraltar is a narrow channel between the southern tip of Spain and the northern coast of Morocco, connecting the Atlantic Ocean with the Mediterranean Sea. At its narrowest it is only about 14 kilometres wide.

On its northern side rises the Rock of Gibraltar, a British territory, and on the African side Jebel Musa. In ancient times these were known as the Pillars of Hercules and marked the edge of the known world. The Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans all sailed through the strait.

Hundreds of ships pass through every day, and ferries cross between Europe and Africa. Water flows in from the Atlantic at the surface and out as a saltier deep current, and migrating birds and whales use the strait. Engineers have long proposed a tunnel or bridge across it.
